dialogue.scene: Reem finds her brother Khalid revising at one o'clock in the morning before an exam.

p1.t: I've got my physics exam tomorrow, so I'm staying up to revise everything one more time.
Honestly, that might not help. Research suggests that sleep helps the brain store what you've learnt.
Says who? I've always revised late and I'm fine.
According to sleep experts, teenagers need eight to ten hours a night. You're getting about five.

p2.t: But one late night won't have an impact on my grade, will it?
There is strong evidence that lack of sleep slows your reactions and weakens your memory.
Where did you read that? It could be some random website.
No, it was a reliable source: a university study our teacher showed us in class.
Fine, you've convinced me. Lights out by eleven.

dialogue.focus: Research suggests that sleep helps the brain store what you've learnt.

dialogue.scene: Turki and his classmate Saad are in a supermarket in Dammam, looking at an energy drink.

p1.t: Look at this can: 'Boosts focus and energy.' Maybe I'll try it before Saturday's match.
Of course the company claims that. They want to sell it. I'd take it with a pinch of salt.
But it says it's packed with vitamins.
Sure, and it's also packed with sugar and caffeine. Check the label.

p2.t: Oh, there's a warning: 'Not recommended for children.' I didn't notice that.
Exactly. Doctors warn that too much caffeine can cause heart problems and poor sleep.
So the advert's a bit misleading, then.
Yes. And our PE teacher pointed out that water and a banana work just as well before a match.
Fine, a banana it is. It's cheaper anyway!

dialogue.scene: Nawaf and his classmate Liam are preparing a geography presentation about water in Saudi Arabia.

p1.t: Let's open with a big fact. Saudi Arabia is thought to be the world's largest producer of desalinated water.
Good start. Do we have a source for that?
Yes, several international reports. It is estimated that a large share of the country's drinking water comes from desalination.
And desalination uses a huge amount of energy, so wasting water is expensive.

p2.t: Next, home consumption. On average, a long shower uses far more water than people realise.
People might say one family saving water is just a drop in the ocean.
True, but if millions of families do it, it really adds up.
Then let's finish with three easy tips: shorter showers, fixing leaks and turning off the tap.

dialogue.scene: Lama and Grace are presenting the results of a survey they did at their own school about sport.

p1.t: We asked 200 students in our school how often they do sport. The figures indicate that girls' participation has nearly doubled since last year.
That's mainly because the school opened a new sports hall. A significant proportion of girls now play basketball after school.
We also asked how students feel before exams.
Students who exercise three times a week reported feeling less stressed.

p2.t: That matches research elsewhere. There is a growing body of evidence that exercise is linked to better mental health.
Of course, our survey was small, so we must be careful.
True, but we can still draw a tentative conclusion: better facilities seem to lead to more active students.
So our recommendation is simple: keep the sports hall open longer.

dialogue.scene: Faisal and Majed are taking part in a youth council discussion about whether their city should build more cycle lanes.

p1.t: I'd like to make the case for more cycle lanes. Research suggests that people cycle more when they feel safe from traffic.
That sounds nice, but isn't it too hot to cycle here for most of the year?
It's a fair point, but it is estimated that many car journeys in cities are shorter than five kilometres.
Is that based on evidence from Saudi cities, though, or from Europe?

p2.t: Mostly from abroad, I admit. My own evidence is anecdotal: since a cycle path opened near us, I've seen far more cyclists.
So that's a strong argument for shaded lanes that people can use after sunset.
Exactly. If we weigh up the evidence, the benefits for health and traffic are clear.
All right, I'm convinced, as long as the lanes have trees and good lighting.

dialogue.scene: Yousef asks his older sister Dana to check an email he is writing to the director of a summer coding camp.

p1.t: Can you check this? 'Hey guys! Wanna know about your camp. Is it expensive? Thx!'
Oh no. That's fine for your friends, but the register is completely wrong for a camp director.
What's wrong with it? It's short and clear.
It sounds rude. Start with 'Dear Mr Carter' and then 'I am writing to enquire about your summer coding camp.'

p2.t: Okay. And instead of 'Is it expensive?'
Try 'I would be grateful if you could tell me the fees.' Then finish with 'I look forward to hearing from you.'
And not 'Thx'?
Definitely not. Write 'Yours sincerely' and your full name. Save 'Speak soon!' for messages to me.
Fine. Just a quick message to my sister, then: thanks!

words.ex: According to our biology teacher, the brain sorts memories while we sleep.
Research suggests that short naps can improve concentration.
There is strong evidence that regular exercise is good for the brain.
Lack of sleep can make it hard to control your mood.
A university website is usually a reliable source.
Sleep has a big impact on how well we learn.

dialogue.t: I've got my physics exam tomorrow, so I'm staying up to revise everything one more time.
Honestly, that might not help. Research suggests that sleep helps the brain store what you've learnt.
But one late night won't have an impact on my grade, will it?
There is strong evidence that lack of sleep slows your reactions and weakens your memory.
Where did you read that? It could be some random website.
No, it was a reliable source: a university study our teacher showed us in class.
Fine, you've convinced me. Lights out by eleven.

grammar.title: Introducing evidence
grammar.ar: نقدّم الدليل بـ According to + اسم المصدر، أو Research suggests that + جملة، أو There is strong evidence that + جملة. لا نقول According to me، بل In my view.
examples: According to the study, students who sleep well get better marks.
Research suggests that screens before bed delay sleep.
There is strong evidence that lack of sleep affects memory.

words.ex: The company claims that its drink improves focus.
Doctors warn that too much caffeine is harmful for teenagers.

words.ar: يُنبّه إلى أنّ / يشير إلى أنّ
words.ex: The coach pointed out that water is the best drink during training.
Dates are packed with natural energy.
The photo on the box was completely misleading.

words.w: take something with a pinch of salt
words.ar: لا تصدّقه تماماً / تتعامل معه بتحفّظ
words.ex: I take online reviews with a pinch of salt.

dialogue.t: Look at this can: 'Boosts focus and energy.' Maybe I'll try it before Saturday's match.
Of course the company claims that. They want to sell it. I'd take it with a pinch of salt.
But it says it's packed with vitamins.
Sure, and it's also packed with sugar and caffeine. Check the label.
Oh, there's a warning: 'Not recommended for children.' I didn't notice that.
Exactly. Doctors warn that too much caffeine can cause heart problems and poor sleep.
So the advert's a bit misleading, then.
Yes. And our PE teacher pointed out that water and a banana work just as well before a match.

grammar.title: Reporting verbs + that
grammar.ar: نستخدم أفعال النقل لنوضّح موقف المصدر: claim (يزعم دون دليل)، warn (يحذّر)، point out (ينبّه إلى حقيقة). كلها تأتي مع that + جملة.
examples: The advert claims that the cream works in a week.
Experts warn that some products contain hidden sugar.
She pointed out that the price had doubled.

words.ex: It is estimated that a leaking tap wastes thousands of litres a year.
Masmak Fort is thought to be over 150 years old.
Water consumption rises sharply in summer.
Desalination uses a lot of energy.
On average, a short shower uses less water than a bath.
One family's savings are a drop in the ocean, but millions of families make a difference.

dialogue.t: Let's open with a big fact. Saudi Arabia is thought to be the world's largest producer of desalinated water.
Good start. Do we have a source for that?
Yes, several international reports. It is estimated that a large share of the country's drinking water comes from desalination.
And desalination uses a huge amount of energy, so wasting water is expensive.
Next, home consumption. On average, a long shower uses far more water than people realise.
People might say one family saving water is just a drop in the ocean.
True, but if millions of families do it, it really adds up.

grammar.title: Impersonal passive
grammar.ar: نستخدم It is estimated/thought/believed that + جملة، أو الفاعل + is thought/said to + فعل، لنقل معلومة دون ذكر من قالها. هذا أسلوب شائع في العروض والكتابة الأكاديمية.
examples: It is estimated that the city uses more water every year.
The fort is thought to be over 150 years old.
Dates are said to be one of the healthiest snacks.

words.ex: The figures indicate that fewer students walk to school.
A significant proportion of students play sport after school.
Good sleep is linked to better grades.
There is a growing body of evidence that time outdoors reduces stress.
Our survey asked 200 students about their hobbies.
It's too early to draw a conclusion from such a small survey.

dialogue.t: We asked 200 students in our school how often they do sport. The figures indicate that girls' participation has nearly doubled since last year.
That's mainly because the school opened a new sports hall. A significant proportion of girls now play basketball after school.
We also asked how students feel before exams.
Students who exercise three times a week reported feeling less stressed.
That matches research elsewhere. There is a growing body of evidence that exercise is linked to better mental health.
Of course, our survey was small, so we must be careful.
True, but we can still draw a tentative conclusion: better facilities seem to lead to more active students.

grammar.title: Talking about data carefully
grammar.ar: مع الأرقام نستخدم indicate / suggest بدل prove لأن الأرقام لا تثبت كل شيء. a proportion of + اسم جمع، و be linked to + اسم أو ‎-ing.
examples: The figures indicate that more girls are joining clubs.
A significant proportion of students cycle to school.
Stress is often linked to lack of sleep.

words.ex: Doctors urge people to drink more water in summer.
The writer admits that recycling isn't the full answer.
The report recommends repairing clothes instead of throwing them away.

words.ar: ينتهي به المطاف في مكبّ النفايات
words.ex: Millions of old shirts end up in landfill every year.
Our teacher emphasised that the deadline was final.
Fast fashion is cheap, but it creates a lot of waste.

dialogue.t: Listen to this. The report emphasises that the fashion industry produces a huge amount of waste every year.
Does it say where all those clothes go?
A lot of them end up in landfill. And the writer admits that recycling isn't the full answer, because many fabrics are hard to recycle.
That's worrying. I buy fast fashion all the time because it's cheap.
Same here. But experts urge people to buy fewer, better-quality clothes.
What else does the report suggest?
It recommends swapping clothes with friends and donating the ones you don't wear.

grammar.title: Reporting verb patterns
grammar.ar: لكل فعل نقل نمطه: urge / advise + شخص + to، recommend / suggest + ‎-ing، admit / emphasise / point out + that. لا نقول: suggest us to buy.
examples: Experts urge shoppers to think before they buy.
The report recommends buying fewer clothes.
The company admitted that it had made mistakes.

words.ex: A good argument is based on evidence, not feelings.
Research suggests that green spaces make people calmer.
It is estimated that the new park will attract thousands of visitors.
That's anecdotal evidence; we need a proper study.
Cost is a strong argument against the plan.
The council weighed up the costs and the benefits.

dialogue.t: I'd like to make the case for more cycle lanes. Research suggests that people cycle more when they feel safe from traffic.
That sounds nice, but isn't it too hot to cycle here for most of the year?
It's a fair point, but it is estimated that many car journeys in cities are shorter than five kilometres.
Is that based on evidence from Saudi cities, though, or from Europe?
Mostly from abroad, I admit. My own evidence is anecdotal: since a cycle path opened near us, I've seen far more cyclists.
So that's a strong argument for shaded lanes that people can use after sunset.
Exactly. If we weigh up the evidence, the benefits for health and traffic are clear.

grammar.title: Building an evidence-based argument
grammar.ar: الحجة القوية = رأي + دليل (Research suggests / It is estimated / According to) + تقييم للدليل (anecdotal أو based on research) + خلاصة (If we weigh up the evidence, …).
examples: Research suggests that shaded streets encourage walking.
My evidence is only anecdotal, but I've noticed a change.
If we weigh up the evidence, the benefits are clear.

words.w: I am writing to enquire about
words.ex: I am writing to enquire about your summer courses.

words.w: I look forward to hearing from you
words.ex: Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.
Dear Ms Lee, … Yours sincerely, Yousef Al-Qahtani
Just a quick message to say thanks for yesterday!
Great to hear from you. Speak soon!
Slang is the wrong register for a job application.

dialogue.t: Can you check this? 'Hey guys! Wanna know about your camp. Is it expensive? Thx!'
Oh no. That's fine for your friends, but the register is completely wrong for a camp director.
What's wrong with it? It's short and clear.
It sounds rude. Start with 'Dear Mr Carter' and then 'I am writing to enquire about your summer coding camp.'
Okay. And instead of 'Is it expensive?'
Try 'I would be grateful if you could tell me the fees.' Then finish with 'I look forward to hearing from you.'
And not 'Thx'?
Definitely not. Write 'Yours sincerely' and your full name. Save 'Speak soon!' for messages to me.

grammar.title: Formal and informal openings and endings
grammar.ar: في الرسالة الرسمية: Dear + اللقب واسم العائلة، جمل كاملة بلا اختصارات، ونختم بـ Yours sincerely. في الرسالة الودية: Hi، اختصارات مثل I'm، ونختم بـ Speak soon.
examples: Dear Dr Al-Harbi, I am writing to enquire about the science club.
Hi Sam! Just a quick message to say good luck tomorrow.
I look forward to hearing from you. Yours sincerely, Noura Al-Saud

words.ex: The match has been postponed because of the weather.
They've put off the trip till next month.
Get in touch when you're back from Jeddah!

words.w: We regret to inform you that
words.ex: We regret to inform you that the course is full.

dialogue.t: Good morning, everyone. We regret to inform you that the trip to the science centre has been postponed due to a sandstorm warning.
Excuse me, sir. Could you tell us when it will take place?
A new date will be announced in due course. For further information, please contact the school office.
Hey Majed! Are we still going to the science centre tomorrow?
Nope, they've put it off because of the sandstorm.
Oh, what a shame. Did they say when?
Not yet. I'll get in touch as soon as I hear anything.

grammar.title: Formal single verbs vs informal phrasal verbs
grammar.ar: الكلام الرسمي يفضّل أفعالاً من كلمة واحدة: postpone, contact, discover, tolerate. الكلام الودي يستخدم الأفعال المركّبة: put off, get in touch, find out, put up with.
examples: The meeting has been postponed. / They've put off the meeting.
Please contact us. / Get in touch!
We discovered the problem. / We found out about the problem.

words.ex: Would you mind if I asked you a question?
I was wondering if you could help me with my project.
Mind if I sit here?
The children were on their best behaviour at the wedding.

words.w: It's an honour to meet you
words.ex: It's an honour to meet you, Dr Saleh.
Let's catch up after dinner!

dialogue.t: It's an honour to meet you, sir. My grandfather often talks about you.
Thank you, young man. I hear you're interested in engineering.
Yes, I am. Would you mind if I asked you for some advice about universities?
With pleasure. In fact, I was wondering if you'd like to visit my old department one day.
Wow, you were on your best behaviour in there!
Of course. Dr Saleh's a really important guest. Mind if I sit here?
Go ahead. So, what did he say?
Loads! Let's catch up properly after dinner.

grammar.title: Polite permission and requests
grammar.ar: كلما زادت الرسمية طالت الجملة: Would you mind if I + فعل ماضٍ؟ / I was wondering if you could + فعل. ومع الأصدقاء نختصر: Mind if I …? / Can I …?
examples: Would you mind if I opened the window?
I was wondering if you could sign my form.
Mind if I borrow your charger?

words.w: I would welcome the opportunity to
words.ar: يسعدني أن تُتاح لي الفرصة لـ
words.ex: I would welcome the opportunity to work with international visitors.
I consider myself a good team player.
She has experience in organising events.
I'm keen to improve my English.
We need reliable volunteers who arrive on time.
Could you elaborate on your role in the project?

dialogue.t: Good afternoon, Noura. Please take a seat. Could you tell me why you'd like to volunteer?
Certainly. I'm keen to help visitors enjoy the event, and I would welcome the opportunity to use my English.
Do you have any experience in this kind of work?
Yes. I have some experience in organising events, as I helped run our school's science fair last year.
Could you elaborate on your role at the science fair?
Of course. I was responsible for welcoming guests and guiding them to the different stands.
And how would your teachers describe you?
I consider myself reliable and calm under pressure. I always arrive early and finish what I start.

grammar.title: Formal spoken language in interviews
grammar.ar: في المقابلة نستخدم جملاً كاملة وكلمات رسمية مثل I consider myself و I would welcome، ونتجنّب العامية مثل yeah و stuff و kind of.

I have experience in working with children.

Thanks for covering for me. I owe you one!

Sorry I missed your party. I'll make it up to you.

dialogue.t: Mrs Hayes, please accept my apologies for missing the deadline yesterday.
Thank you, Rakan. What happened?
It was due to a problem with my laptop, but I should have saved a copy. I apologise for any inconvenience caused to the group.
Rakan! We waited ages for your slides!
I know, my bad. My laptop died and I hadn't backed anything up.
Well, I finished the conclusion for you.
Seriously? Thanks, I owe you one. I'll make it up to you, I promise. Shawarma's on me tomorrow.

grammar.title: Formal and informal apologies
grammar.ar: الاعتذار الرسمي: Please accept my apologies for + ‎-ing / I apologise for …. الاعتذار الودي: Sorry! / My bad / I'll make it up to you. نستخدم due to في الرسمي و because of في الكلام العادي.
examples: Please accept my apologies for the mistake.
I apologise for any inconvenience caused.
Sorry, my bad! I'll make it up to you.

words.ex: On behalf of our class, thank you for coming.
We would be delighted if you could join us.
Fancy coming to the bake sale?
Kindly reply by the end of the week.
It'd be great if you could bring some cookies.

words.w: I look forward to hearing from you
words.ex: Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.

dialogue.t: Let's write to the bakery owner first: 'Dear Mr Al-Otaibi, on behalf of Year 11, I would like to invite you to our bake sale.'
Good. Then: 'We would be delighted if you could donate some pastries.'
And 'Kindly reply by Thursday.' Then we finish with 'I look forward to hearing from you.'
Perfect. Now the message to our friends. No 'kindly' there!
Ha, true. 'Hey everyone! Fancy helping at our bake sale on Saturday?'
'It'd be great if you could bring some homemade cookies. All the money goes to charity!'
Done. Two messages, the same news, totally different styles.

grammar.title: Changing register
grammar.ar: الرسمي: on behalf of / We would be delighted if / kindly. الودي: Fancy + ‎-ing / It'd be great if / Let me know. نغيّر الكلمات وطول الجملة حسب المستمع.
examples: On behalf of the team, we would be delighted if you could attend.
Fancy coming to the match on Friday?
It'd be great if you could bring your camera.

words.ex: It might be worth asking the students what they think.
What if we opened a second counter?
We need to tackle the problem of litter in the playground.
That could work, but it might be expensive.
The narrow gate is a bottleneck at home time.
Staggered break times would make the canteen less crowded.

dialogue.t: Okay, let's tackle the canteen problem. Students are waiting fifteen minutes and missing half their break.
The bottleneck is the payment counter. Everyone pays in cash, so it's really slow.
It might be worth letting students pay with their school ID cards.
That could work, but it would take time to set up.
What if we had staggered breaks? Younger students could eat first, and older students ten minutes later.
I like that. It would cut the queue in half, and it wouldn't cost anything.

grammar.title: It might be worth + -ing / What if we …?
grammar.ar: It might be worth بعدها فعل ‎-ing لاقتراح لطيف غير مباشر. What if we بعدها مضارع (What if we start …?) أو ماضٍ ليصبح الاقتراح أكثر تحفّظاً (What if we started …?).
examples: It might be worth checking the prices first.
What if we start the meeting earlier?
What if we asked the parents to help?

words.ex: I'd suggest that we ask parents for help.
I'd like to propose a charity football match.
We could cut costs by sharing buses with another school.
The club raised funds by selling homemade food.
A local sports shop agreed to be our sponsor.
The trip went over budget because of the hotel.

dialogue.t: Here's the problem: new kits and the trip to the Dammam tournament would cost twice our budget.
Then we need to cut costs. I'd suggest that we keep last year's kits for one more season.
That would save a lot, but some shirts are really worn out.
Fine. What if we only replaced the damaged ones?
Good. Even so, we'll go over budget with the trip.
Then let's raise funds. I'd like to propose a five-a-side tournament for parents and teachers. They pay to enter.
Brilliant. And supposing we found a sponsor, like the sports shop near school?

grammar.title: suggest / propose
grammar.ar: بعد suggest أو propose نستخدم ‎-ing (I suggest asking …) أو that we + فعل مجرّد (I'd suggest that we ask …). لا نقول: I suggest us to ask.
examples: I'd suggest that we ask a local company.
I propose holding a bake sale.
Supposing we found a sponsor, could we afford the trip?

words.ex: Have we considered using the metro?
I can't see that working because it's too expensive.
The beauty of this plan is that it costs nothing.
My father drops me off on his way to work.
More buses would help ease congestion in the city centre.

dialogue.t: Every morning, cars block the street for twenty minutes. It's dangerous, and it has a knock-on effect on the whole neighbourhood.
Most of the problem is parents stopping right at the gate to drop off their children.
Some parents suggested building a bigger car park.
I can't see that working, to be honest. It would take years and cost a fortune.
So what do you propose?
Have we considered a 'walking bus'? Parents drop children at the nearby mall car park, and teachers walk them to school in a group.
Interesting. The beauty of it is that it costs almost nothing.

grammar.title: Evaluating proposals
grammar.ar: للتقييم الإيجابي: The beauty of it is that …. للرفض المهذّب: I can't see that working because …. لطرح فكرة جديدة: Have we considered + اسم أو ‎-ing؟
examples: Have we considered sharing cars?
I can't see that working because the road is too narrow.
The beauty of it is that everyone can join in.

words.ex: Smaller plates? That's worth a try.

dialogue.t: Last Eid, we threw away trays of rice and meat. I hate seeing food go to waste.
Same. What if we just cooked less this year?
The trouble with that is that Grandma will worry there isn't enough for the guests.
True. Hospitality matters to her. It might be worth asking the guests to confirm if they're coming.
That's worth a try. And what about the leftovers?
A food bank in our city collects good food from events and gives it to families in need.
It would mean organising boxes and a pickup, but I think it's worth it.

words.ex: Right, let's get down to business.

Are we all agreed that we'll meet again on Sunday?

Each action point has a name and a deadline.

dialogue.t: Right, let's get down to business. The first item on the agenda is where to go for the end-of-year trip.
I'd suggest the aquarium in Jeddah. Everyone's been talking about it.
It might be worth looking at the cost first. The bus alone is expensive.
Good point. Shall we move on to the budget and come back to this later?
Agreed.
Fine by me. Should we take a vote on the date as well?
Yes, quickly. Hands up for the 15th. Right, that's decided. Action points: Luke contacts the bus companies, and Waleed books the tickets.

words.ex: It might be worth asking the neighbours first.

dialogue.t: Let's get down to business. Teenagers here say there's nowhere to go in the evenings. Any ideas?
What if we turned the empty hall next to the park into a youth centre?
I like it, but is it a feasible option? Renovating it would cost a lot.
It might be worth running a pilot scheme first, maybe two evenings a week with games and study tables.
The beauty of a pilot is that we can see if people actually come. But what about noise for the neighbours?
We need to strike a balance. If we close by ten, it shouldn't disturb anyone.
To recap: a three-month pilot, two evenings a week, closing at ten. Have we reached a consensus?

grammar.title: Meeting language: the full cycle

examples: What if we ran a pilot scheme for three months?
Is that a feasible option with our budget?
To recap, we'll start in March. Have we reached a consensus?

The person I've chosen to talk about is my uncle Majid, who's a paramedic in Riyadh.
I've always looked up to him because he stays calm in situations that would terrify most people.
What's more, he goes out of his way to help our neighbours, even on his days off.
Last year he taught first aid at my school, which meant that dozens of students learnt basic life-saving skills.
He's a real role model, and that class left a lasting impression on me. It's partly why I want to study medicine.

dialogue.t: Okay, two minutes, starting now. Describe a place you'd like to visit.
Japan has been on my bucket list for years, especially the city of Kyoto.
What really appeals to me is the mix of old and new.
A good example of this is the way traditional wooden houses stand next to ultra-modern train stations.
Having said that, I don't only want to see the famous sights. I'd like to go somewhere off the beaten track, too.
I've read about small mountain villages where the scenery is breathtaking, especially in autumn.
Time's up! Great examples. Maybe add why the trip matters to you personally.

grammar.ar: قبل اسم أو قائمة أسماء نستخدم such as. ولتقديم مثال كامل نستخدم A good example of this is + اسم أو جملة (the way …). الأمثلة تجعل الإجابة الطويلة أقوى.
examples: I love outdoor sports such as hiking and kayaking.

What really appeals to me is the history of the place.

words.ex: Looking back, it was the best decision I've made.
Can you lend me a hand with these boxes?
At the time, I was too nervous to speak.
Out of the blue, my old friend called me.
Teaching my little brother to read was really rewarding.
A kind word can make all the difference.

dialogue.t: Describe a time when you helped someone. You have two minutes.
I was waiting for my flight when, out of the blue, a woman asked me for help. She had missed her connection.
At the time, I was nervous about speaking English to a stranger, but I decided to lend a hand.
I went with her to the airline desk and helped her explain the problem, which meant that she got a seat on the next flight.
She said my help made all the difference, and she even sent me a thank-you email later.
Looking back, it was one of the most rewarding things I've ever done. It also gave me confidence in my English.

grammar.title: Signposts in a story
grammar.ar: لترتيب القصة في الإجابة المطوّلة: At the time (وقتها)، Out of the blue (فجأة)، ثم نتيجة بـ which meant that، ونختم بتأمّل: Looking back, …. ونستخدم أزمنة الماضي التي درستها سابقاً.
examples: At the time, I didn't know what to do.
Out of the blue, the lights went out.
Looking back, I learnt a lot from that day.

words.ex: The test was hard. Having said that, I enjoyed it.

words.w: It's not that …, it's just that …
words.ex: It's not that I don't like football, it's just that I prefer swimming.

On the whole, the trip was a success.

dialogue.t: Do you think famous people have a responsibility to be good role models?
That's a tricky question. To some extent, yes, because millions of young people follow them online.
Having said that, it's not that celebrities are bad people, it's just that nobody can be perfect all the time.
Who are better role models for teenagers: celebrities or family members?
On the whole, I'd say family members. You see how they deal with real problems every day.
Has this changed compared to the past?
I think so. In my grandparents' time, role models were mostly local people, whereas now they can be anyone in the world.

grammar.title: Balancing and contrasting in Part 3
grammar.ar: في الجزء الثالث نوازن الإجابة: To some extent … ثم Having said that, …. ونقارن بـ By contrast, … أو whereas. ونوضّح السبب الحقيقي بـ It's not that …, it's just that ….
examples: To some extent, yes. Having said that, there are exceptions.
Cities are noisy. By contrast, villages are peaceful.
It's not that I'm lazy, it's just that I'm tired.

words.ex: Compared to my parents' generation, we travel much more.

dialogue.t: How have people's shopping habits changed in your country?
Hugely. Compared to when my parents were young, there's been a shift towards online shopping, especially for clothes and electronics.
Why do you think that is?
Mainly convenience. Delivery is fast, and you don't have to drive in the summer heat.
Do you think traditional markets will disappear?
I'd imagine that some small shops will become a thing of the past.
Having said that, souqs are part of our culture, so I think they'll survive as places to meet and explore.

grammar.title: Comparing past, present and future
grammar.ar: للماضي: used to + فعل. للتغيّر حتى الآن: There's been a shift towards …. للمقارنة: Compared to …, whereas …. وللتوقّع: I'd imagine that … will …
examples: Compared to the past, families eat out more often.

words.ex: I picked up some Spanish on holiday.
I finally got the hang of riding a bike.

To wrap up, it's a skill worth learning.
He moved abroad, which meant that I had to find a new coach.

dialogue.t: Now, describe a skill you would like to learn. You've had one minute to prepare.
The skill I'd most like to pick up is falconry, which is a traditional sport in Saudi Arabia.
My grandfather trained falcons when he was young, but he stopped years ago, which meant that nobody in the family learnt it from him.
I know it has a steep learning curve. It can take months to get the hang of training a falcon.
Thank you. Do you think traditional skills are still important for young people?
Definitely. They connect us to our history. Having said that, young people also need modern skills, such as coding.
Is it better to learn skills from a teacher or online?
It depends on the skill. You can pick up coding online, whereas something like falconry needs a real expert beside you.

pages.text: Faisal had expected the summer to be unbearably dull. His parents had sent him to stay with his grandfather on the Farasan Islands, a scattering of coral islands in the Red Sea, where the internet was patchy at best and the nearest shopping mall was a ferry ride away. For the first three days, he wandered around the house at a loose end, holding his phone up towards the sky as if it might catch a stronger signal. "You won't find anything worth seeing on that little screen," his grandfather, Abu Saleh, remarked one evening as he mended a fishing net. "Come with me tonight, and I'll show you something most people never get to witness."

Just before midnight, they walked down to a quiet beach on the southern side of the island, the sand still warm beneath their sandals. Abu Saleh switched off his torch the moment they arrived and told Faisal to do the same with his phone. "Turtles find their way by the moonlight reflecting on the water," he whispered. "Anything brighter confuses them." As Faisal's eyes gradually adjusted to the darkness, he made out a huge shape dragging itself slowly up the beach. It was a hawksbill turtle, her shell patterned like polished amber, and she had come ashore to lay her eggs.

They watched in silence from a respectful distance as the turtle dug a deep hole with her back flippers. It took her nearly an hour, and by the time she had covered her eggs and returned to the waves, Faisal had completely lost track of time. "She may have hatched on this very beach thirty years ago," Abu Saleh said quietly. "They always come back to the place where they were born, no matter how far they've travelled." Faisal found the idea strangely moving. He had never imagined that an animal could remember home.

Over the following weeks, Faisal threw himself into learning everything he could about turtles. His grandfather introduced him to Dr Hassan, a marine biologist from the national wildlife authority, who explained that hawksbills were critically endangered and that only about one hatchling in a thousand survived to adulthood. The eggs, he said, would hatch in roughly two months, and the babies would instinctively head for the brightest horizon, which on a natural beach is always the sea. However, a new seafront restaurant had recently opened just above the nesting beach, decorated with strings of dazzling white lights. "If those lights are still on when the eggs hatch," Dr Hassan warned, frowning, "we could be in serious trouble."

The night of the hatching arrived sooner than anyone had predicted. Faisal was sitting on the sand with his grandfather and Dr Hassan when the surface of the nest began to tremble and then collapse. Within seconds, dozens of tiny turtles, each no bigger than a matchbox, came tumbling out and scrambled across the sand. But instead of heading towards the dark, glittering water, they turned the other way. To Faisal's horror, they were crawling straight towards the glowing restaurant and the busy road beside it.

Without stopping to think, Faisal sprinted up the beach and burst into the restaurant, completely out of breath. "Please, you have to turn off your lights right now!" he begged the manager, a tall man who looked rather taken aback. "I've got a restaurant full of customers, young man," the manager replied, folding his arms. "I can't just plunge everyone into darkness." Faisal took a deep breath and explained, as calmly as he could, that over a hundred endangered baby turtles would die within minutes unless the lights went out. An elderly customer put down his tea and said firmly, "The boy is right, and I'd happily eat my dinner by candlelight to save them."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room, and the manager finally gave in and reached for the switch. Instantly, the seafront was plunged into darkness, and the moon, which had been hidden behind the glare all evening, suddenly seemed to shine twice as brightly on the waves. Back on the beach, the hatchlings hesitated, as if they were reconsidering their journey. Then, one by one, they turned around and began scrambling towards the silver water. Dr Hassan carefully collected the few that had already reached the edge of the road and set them gently down near the shoreline.

Faisal stood at the water's edge and watched the last tiny turtle disappear into the foam. Dr Hassan counted the empty eggshells and announced that a hundred and twelve hatchlings had made it safely into the sea. Several customers had come down from the restaurant to watch, and some of them were quietly wiping their eyes. Abu Saleh rested his hand on his grandson's shoulder. "If you hadn't acted so quickly, Faisal, not a single one of them would have survived tonight," he said, his voice full of pride.

The following morning, the restaurant manager knocked on Abu Saleh's door and promised to replace his bright white bulbs with soft amber lights that would not disturb the turtles. He even asked Faisal to help him design a sign explaining to customers why the seafront stayed dim during the nesting season. When the time came to return to Riyadh at the end of the summer, Faisal surprised everyone, including himself, by not wanting to leave. As the ferry pulled away, he gazed back at the shrinking islands and made himself a quiet promise. Like the turtles, he would always find his way back.

pages.text: The studio lights were so bright that Layla could barely see the audience, but she could feel hundreds of eyes on her. She had made it to the final of Young Chefs of the Kingdom, and she had practised her saffron chicken kabsa until she could cook it in her sleep. Then the head judge, Chef Mansour, stepped forward and announced a surprise theme: "Cook the dish your grandmother is famous for." Layla's heart sank, because there was only one possible answer. Her grandmother was famous for jareesh, and jareesh took at least four hours to cook properly. The clock on the wall read ninety minutes.

Standing at her counter, Layla found herself back in her grandmother's kitchen in Qassim, where the air always smelled of ghee and cardamom. She remembered sitting on a stool while her grandmother stirred the thick pot of crushed wheat, never once hurrying. "Food that is rushed tastes of hurry," her grandmother used to say, tapping the wooden spoon on the edge of the pot. Layla had laughed at the time, thinking it was just one of those things old people say. Now, with the cameras rolling, those words felt more like a warning.

At the next counter, Sultan, the boy everyone expected to win, was already slicing vegetables at lightning speed for something quick and elegant. Layla could have played it safe and cooked something simpler, but it would not have been honest to the theme. Taking a deep breath, she reached for the pressure cooker instead. If she could not give the wheat four hours, she would have to force it to cook faster. One of the judges raised an eyebrow, clearly doubting whether she knew what she was doing.

For forty minutes, everything went according to plan, and the pressure cooker hissed steadily like a contented cat. However, when Layla finally released the steam and lifted the lid, a sharp, bitter smell rose into the air. The wheat at the bottom had stuck to the pan and burnt, while she had been busy preparing the onions. A camera swung towards her, and she heard a murmur ripple through the audience. Her hands began to shake, and for a terrible moment she considered switching off the heat and simply walking away.

Then another memory came to her rescue: the day her grandmother had burnt a pot of rice before a family wedding. Instead of panicking, she had calmly spooned the top layer into a clean pot, refusing to touch the blackened bottom. "Never scrape a burnt pot," she had explained, "or you will spread the bitterness through everything." Layla grabbed a fresh pan and, with surprising steadiness, lifted out only the soft, creamy wheat from the top. She added a splash of milk, some butter and a pinch of salt, and stirred slowly, just as her grandmother would have done.

With fifteen minutes left, Layla realised to her horror that she had run out of onions for the golden topping. Before she could even ask, Sultan slid a bowl of his spare onions across to her counter without saying a word. "We're competing, not fighting," he muttered with a half-smile, before turning back to his own plate. Layla was too grateful to reply, so she simply nodded and got to work. She fried the onions until they were dark and sweet, then finished the dish with crushed dried lime and a spoonful of melted ghee.

When the bell rang, Layla stepped back, her apron stained and her face burning from the heat. Chef Mansour took his time, tasting her jareesh slowly while the whole studio held its breath. He frowned and asked, "There's a faint smokiness here, isn't there? Did you add it on purpose?" Layla could have pretended it was a clever chef's trick, and nobody would ever have found out. Instead, she told him the truth: the bottom had burnt, and she had rescued what she could.

To her astonishment, Chef Mansour's frown softened into a smile. "When I was a boy, my grandmother cooked jareesh over a wood fire, and it always had exactly this taste," he said quietly. "You made a mistake, but you didn't throw the pot away, and you handled it like a real cook." He added that any chef can follow a recipe, but very few can think clearly when things go wrong. Layla blinked hard, determined not to cry in front of the entire country.

Half an hour later, Layla was holding the winner's trophy, while Sultan, who had come a close second, was the first to shake her hand. As soon as she reached the backstage area, her phone buzzed with a call from Qassim. "I watched every minute," her grandmother said, her voice full of pride. "You were honest, and you didn't give up on the pot." Then she laughed and added, "But next time, come home and cook jareesh with me properly, all four hours of it." Layla promised she would, and for once she was in no hurry at all.

pages.text: In the old quarter of Jeddah, behind a carved wooden door, stood a coral-stone house that Faisal's uncle Hamza had turned into a small museum. Faisal, who was sixteen, had spent the whole afternoon polishing its most precious object: a brass astrolabe crafted in the thirteenth century to measure the positions of the stars. The polish was thick and grey, and by the time he had finished, his fingertips were stained so darkly that no amount of scrubbing could clean them. "Leave them," his uncle laughed. "Those are the hands of a man who respects history." Neither of them could have guessed that a few dark smudges would soon matter more than anything else in the building.

That evening, the museum held a small reception for a group of visitors and experts. Among them was Dr. Samir Nadeem, a smartly dressed consultant who advised private collectors and who had already asked three times about the astrolabe's value. Tariq, the new guide, was nervously serving Arabic coffee, while Mr. Haroon, the caretaker who had worked there for thirty years, watched quietly from the doorway. At exactly twenty to nine, just as Uncle Hamza raised his hand to begin his speech, every light in the house went out. Someone gasped, a cup shattered on the tiled floor, and the hall was swallowed by darkness.

The blackout lasted no more than three minutes, but when the lights flickered back on, the glass case in the centre of the room was standing open. The astrolabe had vanished. Uncle Hamza, pale but surprisingly calm, locked the front door at once and phoned the police. Within half an hour, Sergeant Al-Otaibi had arrived and searched every guest, every bag and every pocket. Nothing was found, and nobody, it seemed, could have left the building.

Suspicion quickly fell on Tariq, who admitted that he had left the hall during the darkness. "I went straight to the fuse box in the courtyard," he insisted, holding up hands that were grey with dust. Dr. Samir shook his head sympathetically and remarked that a new employee would certainly know where the keys to the case were kept. Several guests began whispering, and Tariq looked as though he wanted the floor to open beneath him. Faisal, however, had read enough detective novels to know that you should never jump to conclusions, especially when someone is so eager to help you reach them.

As the sergeant took statements, Faisal stood quietly in a corner, thinking. If the astrolabe was not in anyone's pocket, then it must still be hidden somewhere inside the house, waiting to be collected later. He glanced down at his own stained fingers and suddenly remembered that the fresh polish rubbed off on anything that touched the brass. Mr. Haroon's hands were spotless, and Tariq's were covered in ordinary dust. But when Dr. Samir lifted his coffee cup, Faisal noticed a faint grey smudge on the white cuff of his shirt.

Pretending to collect the broken pieces of the cup, Faisal moved slowly around the hall, examining every surface. In the far corner stood an enormous antique dallah, a brass coffee pot so large that no one had ever used it for coffee. On its lid, almost invisible, was a grey fingerprint exactly like the ones on his own hands. Holding his breath, he lifted the lid and saw, wrapped in a silk handkerchief, the gleaming astrolabe. At that moment the penny dropped: the thief had never intended to walk out with it that night.

Faisal whispered his discovery to his uncle and the sergeant in the small office at the back. "If we accuse Dr. Samir now, he'll simply claim that anyone could have touched the pot," Sergeant Al-Otaibi pointed out. "We need to catch him red-handed." Faisal remembered that Dr. Samir had generously offered to return early the next morning to "assess any damage to the collection." So they replaced the astrolabe exactly where it had been, hid a tiny camera behind a lantern, and told the guests that the investigation would continue the following day.

At half past seven the next morning, Dr. Samir arrived, looking fresh and full of concern. He asked politely whether he might spend a few minutes alone in the hall to concentrate on his report. The moment the door closed behind him, he walked straight to the corner, lifted the lid of the dallah and reached inside. "Looking for something, Doctor?" asked Sergeant Al-Otaibi, stepping out from behind a tall wooden screen. Dr. Samir froze, his hand still inside the coffee pot, and for once he had absolutely nothing clever to say.

Later he confessed that a buyer abroad had offered him a fortune, and that he had loosened the main fuse that afternoon so the lights would fail on time. Tariq received a sincere apology from everyone who had doubted him, and Mr. Haroon made him the best coffee of his life. Uncle Hamza added a new line to the astrolabe's description card: "Recovered by Faisal Al-Harbi, assistant curator." That night, Faisal looked up at the stars over the old city and smiled. The astrolabe had been made to measure the heavens, but it had taught him to measure people by evidence rather than appearances.

pages.text: Yusuf Al-Harbi had a secret that nobody, not even his parents, had ever guessed. Once a day, for exactly sixty seconds, he could make the whole world stand still. Cars froze mid-turn, birds hung in the air like decorations, and the steam from his mother's coffee pot stopped as if painted on glass. He had discovered this ability two years earlier, at thirteen, when he dropped his grandfather's favourite cup and found himself catching it in a silent, motionless kitchen.

Since then, he had become something of an urban legend in Riyadh. People spoke of a mysterious figure who appeared out of nowhere: a child pulled back from a busy road, a wallet returned before its owner had even noticed it was missing. Social media called him "The Minute", and his classmates argued endlessly about who he might be. Yusuf would simply keep his head down and carry on with his maths homework, trying hard not to smile. However, there was one thing the rumours never mentioned: sixty seconds is far shorter than it sounds.

His grandfather, the only person who had worked out the truth, often reminded him of this. "A minute is a gift, not a kingdom," he would say, sipping his tea on the roof as the call to prayer drifted across the city. Yusuf found these sayings rather old-fashioned. After all, he had never once failed to solve a problem in time. If he was honest, he had begun to believe that he could handle anything on his own.

That belief was put to the test on a windy Thursday afternoon in March. Yusuf was walking home past a huge construction site when a sudden sandstorm swept in, turning the sky the colour of rust. Above him, a tall crane groaned and began to swing out of control, its heavy load of steel beams swaying towards a crowded bus stop. Workers shouted and people ran in all directions, and in the middle of the chaos Yusuf spotted a little boy who had let go of his father's hand. Without a second thought, he stopped time.

The silence was instant and total. Yusuf sprinted towards the bus stop, counting under his breath, and lifted the boy into his father's arms. Forty-eight seconds left. But when he looked up, his heart sank: there were at least twenty people beneath the swaying beams, and many more on the pavement nearby. Even if he could carry one person every two seconds, which was impossible through the thick, frozen sand, he would never get them all to safety.

For a moment he panicked, and precious seconds slipped away. Then his grandfather's voice came back to him: a gift, not a kingdom. Yusuf realised that he did not need to save everyone himself; he only needed to give others the chance to do it. He climbed the ladder to the crane's cabin as fast as his legs would allow, and there sat the operator, frozen, his face twisted with fear, his hand inches away from the emergency brake. Gently, Yusuf placed the man's fingers on the red lever.

Twenty seconds remained. He raced back down, pulled the fire alarm on the site office wall so that it would ring the moment time returned, and turned a security guard so that he faced the bus stop instead of the gate. Finally, he pressed a loudspeaker into the hands of a foreman whose mouth was already open in mid-shout. With three seconds to spare, Yusuf ducked behind a concrete wall, breathless, and let go.

The world exploded back into noise. The operator, feeling the lever under his hand, pulled it instinctively, and the crane jerked to a halt. The alarm screamed, the guard saw the danger at once and began waving people away, and the foreman's voice boomed through the loudspeaker, directing the crowd towards the open street. Within moments everyone was clear, and when the beams finally slid to the ground with a deafening crash, they landed on nothing but empty pavement.

The next morning, the news was full of praise for the crane operator, the guard and the foreman, who were being called "the heroes of the sandstorm". Not a single report mentioned The Minute, and for once Yusuf did not mind in the slightest. That evening, he joined his grandfather on the roof and told him everything. The old man listened in silence, then poured him a cup of tea. "So," he said with a knowing smile, "you have finally learned how long a minute really is." "Long enough," Yusuf replied, "if you don't spend it alone."

pages.text: Faisal had made it perfectly clear that he didn't want to come. Every winter, his grandfather insisted on a family camping trip to the Hisma desert near Tabuk, and every winter Faisal complained that there was nothing to do there. This year, with his phone barely holding onto a single bar of signal, he was even less enthusiastic than usual. His cousin Saad, who was a year younger, seemed thrilled by the empty red dunes stretching endlessly towards the horizon. "You'll thank me one day," Grandfather said with a knowing smile, as if he could read Faisal's mind.

By the time the sun had set, the tents were up and a fire was crackling between the rocks. Grandfather poured cardamom coffee into small cups while the sky slowly filled with more stars than Faisal had ever seen in Riyadh. Pointing upwards, the old man asked whether either of the boys could find the North Star. "I don't need to," Faisal replied, holding up his phone. "I've got an app that tells me exactly where everything is." Grandfather didn't argue; he simply raised an eyebrow and took a slow sip of his coffee.

Instead, he told them about his own father, who had crossed this desert on camels long before anyone had heard of satellites. "He used to say that the sky is a map that never runs out of battery," Grandfather explained. He showed them how to follow the stars of Banat Na'sh to find the North Star, which never moves from its place. He also pointed out the ripples in the sand, shaped by a wind that almost always blew from the same direction. Saad listened eagerly, but Faisal only half paid attention, scrolling through photos he couldn't even upload.

Long before dawn, Faisal shook Saad awake with a plan. A famous sandstone arch stood somewhere to the north, and he was determined to film the sunrise from the top of it. Saad was hesitant, so Faisal left a quick note on Grandfather's bag to reassure him that they would be back for breakfast. They set off in the cold darkness, following the blue dot on Faisal's screen. As they walked, Faisal couldn't help noticing a bright star shining straight ahead of them, exactly where Grandfather had said it would be.

The sunrise was breathtaking, and for a few minutes Faisal forgot all about his followers. Then, almost without warning, the wind picked up and a thick haze of dust began swirling across the dunes. When Faisal reached for his phone to check the route back, the screen flickered once and went completely black. The freezing night had drained the battery far faster than he had expected. Saad's face fell as he admitted that he had left his own phone charging in the tent.

Within minutes, the arch behind them had disappeared into the dust, and every dune looked exactly like the next. Saad wanted to start running in the direction he thought was right, but Faisal grabbed his arm. "If we panic, we'll only get more lost," he said, trying to keep a cool head even though his heart was pounding. He closed his eyes and forced himself to remember the walk out. The star had been ahead of them the whole way, which meant the camp had to be directly behind them, to the south.

The stars had long since faded, but through the haze the sun was still visible as a pale, silver disc. "If we're walking south, the sunrise should be on our left," Faisal reasoned aloud, and suddenly the penny dropped for Saad too. They kept the faint sun on their left shoulders and checked that they were crossing the sand ripples at the same angle as before. Every few hundred steps they stopped to make sure they hadn't drifted off course. Doubt crept in more than once, yet neither of them dared to say it out loud.

After nearly an hour, Saad stopped suddenly and sniffed the air. It was smoke, unmistakable and sharp, carried towards them on the wind. A moment later they spotted a thin grey column rising above the next dune, much darker than the dust around it. Grandfather had thrown green branches onto the fire on purpose, turning it into a signal that could be seen from far away. The boys scrambled up the final slope and almost collapsed with relief at the sight of the familiar tents.

Grandfather wasn't angry, but his quiet silence was somehow worse than shouting would have been. Faisal apologised sincerely, admitting that he had been far too confident and stubborn. "You remembered the star and the sun when it mattered," the old man said at last, squeezing his shoulder. "The desert is a patient teacher, but it doesn't forgive easily." That night, Faisal left his phone in the tent and sat by the fire, asking his grandfather to name every star he knew.

pages.text: When the school announced that the old library was being renovated, Yousef volunteered to help, mainly because it meant missing two periods of geography. He spent the morning carrying dusty boxes and pulling ancient encyclopaedias off the shelves. Behind the very last bookcase, wedged against the wall, he found a thin blue notebook that had clearly been forgotten for years. The cover said only "S.H. – 1998" in neat, careful handwriting. Inside were thirty-nine maths problems, each one solved with remarkable patience, and then a fortieth problem with nothing beneath it but a single sentence: "I could not solve this one. If you can, you are braver than I was."

At break, Yousef showed the notebook to his two closest friends, Hamad and Turki. "Braver?" Hamad said, raising an eyebrow. "It's a maths problem, not a lion." Problem Forty asked how many different routes a knight could take across a strange, irregular board without landing on the same square twice. It looked simple at first glance, which, as Turki pointed out, was exactly what made it suspicious. By the time the bell rang, all three of them were hooked.

For the next week, the boys spent every spare minute on the problem. They filled pages with diagrams, argued in the canteen, and messaged each other late into the night until their parents told them to put their phones away. Every approach they tried seemed promising for a while and then collapsed completely. "We've hit a dead end," Hamad admitted on Thursday, rubbing his tired eyes. "Maybe we should stop trying to solve it and start trying to find the person who wrote it." It was a long shot, but it was better than giving up.

The school secretary, Mr. Nasser, looked amused when they asked to see the yearbook from 1998. He disappeared into a storeroom and returned with a heavy album whose pages had turned slightly yellow with age. Together they searched through rows of serious faces in old-fashioned photographs, looking for anyone with the initials S.H. There were three possibilities, but only one name made Yousef's heart skip a beat: Saleh Al-Harbi. "That's impossible," Turki whispered. "That's the name of our maths teacher."

Mr. Saleh was the quietest teacher in the school, a calm man who rarely raised his voice and never seemed to be in a hurry. The next morning, Yousef casually mentioned knight problems during class, watching carefully for any reaction. For a moment, the teacher's chalk stopped moving on the board, and something unreadable crossed his face. Then he simply said, "Interesting topic. Page sixty-two, everyone," and carried on as though nothing had happened. After the lesson, the three friends agreed that they could not ask him directly, at least not until they had something worth showing him.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. Turki, who had been playing chess with his grandfather for years, suddenly realised that they had been looking at the problem the wrong way round. "Chess players don't always plan from the start," he explained excitedly. "Sometimes they imagine the final position and work backwards." Once they began at the last square instead of the first, the confusing paths started to untangle one by one. Late on Sunday evening, after checking their answer three times, they finally wrote it down in the empty space beneath Problem Forty.

On Monday they arrived at school early, before the morning assembly had even started. Yousef placed the blue notebook on Mr. Saleh's desk, open at the last page, with a small note that read: "We think we've done it. Were we brave enough?" None of them could concentrate during the first two lessons, and Hamad kept glancing at the door as if expecting it to burst open. By lunchtime, nothing had happened, and they began to wonder whether they had made a terrible mistake.

Just before the final bell, Mr. Saleh asked the three boys to stay behind. He held the notebook gently, as though it might fall apart in his hands. "I was sixteen when I wrote this," he said quietly. "I had been preparing for the national maths competition, and when I couldn't solve that problem, I convinced myself I wasn't good enough, so I hid the notebook and withdrew." He explained that a wise teacher later told him that an unsolved problem is not a locked door but an open one, waiting for someone to walk through. "I became a teacher because of those words," he added with a small smile, "and it seems I needed to hear them again today."

Two weeks later, Mr. Saleh registered Yousef, Hamad and Turki for the national maths competition, and he offered to train them himself after school. On their first afternoon of practice, he picked up a fresh piece of chalk and wrote a single heading on the board: "Problem Forty-One." The boys exchanged nervous, delighted glances. "I have no idea how to solve this one," their teacher admitted cheerfully. "Shall we find out together?" And for the first time in twenty-five years, the blue notebook had a new page.

pages.text: Faisal had heard the story about the camel and the broken water bag at least thirty times, and he could probably have recited it word for word. Whenever his grandfather began it at dinner, Faisal would quietly roll his eyes and reach for his phone. Lately, though, Jaddi had been forgetting things that mattered more than old stories: where he had parked, whether he had taken his medicine, even his own neighbour's name. A week earlier, after he had got lost driving home from the mosque, Faisal's father had gently but firmly taken away his car keys. Nobody in the house had said much about it since, but the silence felt heavier than any argument.

When the weather finally turned cool, the family packed the car for their annual winter camping trip in the desert north of Riyadh. Faisal's mother and his little sister, Reem, set up the kitchen tent, while his father and uncle unloaded firewood and blankets. "Keep an eye on Jaddi this evening," his father murmured to him. "He's been a bit restless." Faisal nodded, although he had been hoping to spend the evening catching up on messages from his friends. Babysitting his grandfather, he thought bitterly, was hardly what he had in mind for the weekend.

Just before sunset, Jaddi stood up and pointed towards a low ridge in the distance. "There used to be an old acacia tree on the other side of that hill," he said. "My father and I rested under it when I was younger than you." Faisal hesitated, but the old man was already walking, so he grabbed a bottle of water and hurried after him. The ridge turned out to be much further away than it looked, and by the time they reached the top, the sky had faded from orange to deep purple. There was no tree, only sand stretching endlessly in every direction.

When Faisal turned around, he realised with a jolt that he could no longer see the glow of the campfire. He pulled out his phone to check the map, only to watch the screen flicker and go black, as the battery had run out completely. His heart began to pound, and a dozen terrible thoughts raced through his mind at once. "We should have stayed at the camp," he snapped, his voice sharper than he had intended. Jaddi, however, simply lowered himself onto the cool sand and looked up at the sky as if he had all the time in the world.

"Panicking never brought anyone home, my son," Jaddi said calmly. "Sit down and let the stars speak." He raised a shaking finger and traced a line across the sky until it stopped at a small, steady light. "That is Al-Jadi, the star that points north," he explained. "Every other star moves around it, but it stays exactly where it is, like a good father." Faisal stared at it, amazed that something so useful had been hanging over his head his whole life without him ever noticing.

As they began walking, Jaddi told the story of his own father, who had guided travellers across this desert long before roads or satellites existed. This time, to his own surprise, Faisal actually listened, asking question after question. He learned how travellers had read the shape of the dunes, how they had used the wind to judge direction, and why they always kept the north star over a particular shoulder. Somewhere in the middle of the story, Faisal realised that the famous camel tale he had heard thirty times was not really about a camel at all. It was about a boy who had refused to give up when everyone else had lost hope.

About an hour later, Jaddi suddenly stopped and looked around, his face full of confusion. "Which way were we going?" he whispered, and for a moment he seemed very small and very old. Faisal's stomach tightened, but instead of panicking, he took a deep breath and searched the sky. "Our camp is south-east of the ridge, and we've been keeping Al-Jadi behind your left shoulder," he said, repeating exactly what his grandfather had taught him. He took the old man's hand and, for the first time in his life, it was Faisal who led the way.

Not long afterwards, two beams of light swept across the dunes, followed by the familiar roar of his father's car. His father jumped out, his face pale with worry, and for a second Faisal braced himself for a furious lecture. Instead, his father pulled them both into a tight embrace and held on for a long time without saying a word. "We've been searching for nearly two hours," his uncle said, shaking his head in disbelief. "How on earth did you find your way back without a phone?" Faisal glanced at his grandfather and smiled. "I had an excellent teacher," he replied.

Later, wrapped in blankets around the fire, the whole family sat drinking sweet tea while Faisal described their adventure. Reem listened with wide eyes, and even his father laughed when Faisal admitted how badly he had panicked at first. "Jaddi may forget where he leaves his glasses," Faisal said quietly, "but he hasn't forgotten anything that really matters." His mother wiped her eyes and squeezed her father-in-law's hand. That night, nobody reached for a phone, and the conversation went on until the fire had burned down to glowing coals.

Back in Riyadh, Faisal set up a small microphone on the coffee table every Friday afternoon after lunch. One by one, he recorded Jaddi's stories about caravans, droughts, weddings and wells, carefully saving each one in a folder called "Our Family's Map." Cousins from Jeddah and Dammam began listening, sending messages full of questions for Jaddi to answer the following week. When Faisal asked why he had never told these stories properly before, the old man chuckled. "I told them many times," he said, with a twinkle in his eye. "But a story only comes alive when somebody finally decides to listen."

pages.text: Faisal Al-Harbi had always believed that his voice was the one thing nobody could steal. At sixteen, he ran a small channel where he reviewed gadgets, and over two years he had uploaded nearly a hundred videos from his bedroom in Jeddah. His followers loved his calm, slightly sarcastic style, and his grandfather, who barely knew how to send a text message, watched every single episode. "You talk too fast," Jiddo would complain, "but I understand the important parts." Faisal never imagined that those hours of recorded speech would one day be turned against the person who loved them most.

It happened on a Thursday evening while Faisal was at football practice. His grandfather's phone rang, and a desperate voice, Faisal's voice, burst through the speaker. "Jiddo, I've had an accident in a friend's car, and if I don't pay for the damage tonight, they'll call the police." The voice was trembling, apologetic and absolutely convincing, right down to the way Faisal always said "honestly" at the start of his sentences. It begged him not to tell anyone and to transfer eight thousand riyals to an account number, which it read out slowly.

Jiddo was already putting on his glasses to open the banking app when something made him pause. In the background of the call, he heard silence where there should have been traffic, voices, or the hum of a busy street. "Where exactly are you, habibi?" he asked gently. The voice hesitated for a fraction of a second too long before answering, "Near the corniche, Jiddo, please hurry." Yet Faisal had never once called the seafront "the corniche"; ever since he was a small child, he had simply called it "the sea."

Instead of sending the money, Jiddo hung up and called Faisal's mother, who immediately phoned the football coach. Within minutes, a confused and sweaty Faisal was standing by the pitch, assuring everyone that he was perfectly fine and had not been anywhere near a car. When he got home, his grandfather played him a recording of the call, which his phone had saved automatically. Faisal felt the hairs on his arms stand up as he listened to himself pleading for help. "That's me," he whispered, "but I never said any of it."

His older brother Khalid, a computer science student at university, recognised the trick straight away. "It's voice cloning," he explained, scrolling through articles on his laptop. "With enough audio, AI software can learn exactly how someone speaks and then say anything you type, in their voice." Faisal stared at his channel's homepage, at the neat rows of thumbnails showing his own smiling face. Without realising it, he had handed criminals a free training course, one video at a time.

For two days, Faisal could hardly eat, and he seriously considered deleting his entire channel. He felt guilty, as though he had personally put his grandfather in danger. Surprisingly, it was Jiddo who talked him out of it over a glass of tea on the balcony. "When I was young, people forged signatures and wrote false letters," he said, waving his hand dismissively. "Thieves will always find new tools, but that doesn't mean honest people should stop speaking."

So Faisal decided to fight back in the way he knew best. Together with Khalid, he reported the account number and the phone number to the authorities and the bank, providing the recording as evidence. Then he spent a week researching how these scams worked, and he even interviewed a cybersecurity specialist who agreed to speak to him by video call. He learned that criminals deliberately create panic to stop their victims from thinking clearly, and that the best defence was surprisingly low-tech.

That weekend, the whole family gathered in the majlis to agree on a secret "safe word" that no stranger could possibly guess. Khalid suggested a random string of numbers, but Jiddo insisted on something more meaningful. In the end, they chose the name of the old fishing boat Jiddo's father had owned in Yanbu, a word that appeared nowhere online. "If anyone calls asking for money," Jiddo announced proudly, "they must tell me the name of the boat first." Faisal's mother laughed and said it was probably the first time in history that a boat had protected a bank account.

A month later, Faisal uploaded the most important video of his life, titled "My Voice Was Stolen: Here's How to Protect Your Family." For the first time, his grandfather appeared beside him on screen, explaining slowly and carefully how he had noticed the tiny mistake. The video was shared by thousands of people, and many followers wrote to say they had created safe words with their own parents and grandparents. Faisal read the comments with a quiet pride he had never felt from reviewing gadgets. Technology, he realised, could copy a voice perfectly, but it could never copy the way a grandfather knows his grandson.

pages.text: In the spring of 1011, fourteen-year-old Yusuf was given a job that nobody else in the market wanted. Every morning, he had to carry bread, dates and water to a locked house near the great mosque of al-Azhar. People whispered that a madman lived inside, a scholar who had once been brilliant but had lost his mind completely. "Leave the basket and run," warned the old baker. "They say he shouts at the walls and tears up his own books." Yusuf needed the money for his family, so he swallowed his fear and knocked on the heavy wooden door.

For the first few weeks, the rumours seemed to be true. The man, whose name was al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham, wandered around the room muttering to himself, his clothes covered in ink and his papers scattered across the floor. Sometimes he laughed at nothing, and once he asked Yusuf very seriously whether the moon was jealous of the sun. Yet something didn't add up. Whenever Yusuf turned to leave, he caught the man watching him with eyes that were sharp, calm and unmistakably intelligent.

One afternoon, Yusuf arrived to find the scholar sitting perfectly still. "Close the shutters, would you?" he said quietly, and his voice sounded completely normal. As the room fell into darkness, Yusuf gasped, because on the far wall a picture had appeared out of nowhere: the street outside, with its camels, merchants and swaying palm trees, all moving silently and upside down. "It's magic!" he whispered. "Not magic," the man replied with a smile, pointing to a tiny hole in the shutter. "It's light, and it has been trying to tell us its secrets for thousands of years."

He explained that light travels from every object in perfectly straight lines, and when those lines pass through a small hole, they cross over and turn the picture upside down. "The famous Greek thinkers believed that our eyes send out rays to touch the world," he said. "But I have tested it again and again, and I'm convinced it's the other way round: light enters the eye." Yusuf frowned and asked how a man could dare to disagree with such great teachers. "Respect them, by all means," said Ibn al-Haytham, "but never accept an idea simply because a famous person wrote it down. Test it, measure it, and let the evidence decide."

"Then why do you pretend to be mad?" Yusuf blurted out before he could stop himself. The scholar sighed and told him the whole story. Years earlier, he had boasted that he could build something to control the floods of the River Nile, and the Caliph in Cairo, a ruler known for his dangerously unpredictable temper, had immediately summoned him. Ibn al-Haytham had travelled south to Aswan with a team of workers, full of confidence, but when he saw the sheer power of the river and the enormous ancient temples along its banks, his heart sank. "If the people who built those wonders couldn't tame the Nile," he said, "I realised I had made a terrible mistake."

He knew that failing the Caliph could cost him his life, so he made a desperate decision. "I began acting as if I had lost my mind," he admitted, "because nobody punishes a madman for a broken promise." The trick had worked, but the price was high: he had been locked in this house, his belongings taken away, with no idea when he might be free. "Being honest about my mistake was the hardest thing I've ever done, even if I could only be honest with myself," he added. Yusuf promised that he would keep the secret, and from that day on he was no longer just a servant but a student.

Over the following years, the dark room became a secret laboratory. Yusuf held candles at different distances, helped polish curved pieces of glass, and wrote down every measurement in careful columns. One winter morning, a royal official arrived without warning to check on the prisoner, and they had only seconds to hide the papers beneath a pile of blankets. Ibn al-Haytham instantly began singing to a cooking pot, while Yusuf rolled his eyes and complained loudly that the old man had been doing it all week. The official shook his head in disgust and left, and the two of them had to bite their lips to keep from bursting out laughing.

In 1021, news spread through Cairo that the Caliph had died. A few days later, Ibn al-Haytham walked out of his house, washed, dressed in clean clothes and speaking so sensibly that his neighbours could hardly believe their ears. "It seems," he told Yusuf with a wink, "that I have made a remarkable recovery." He spent the following years turning his notes into a great work, the Book of Optics, which explained how light behaves and how we see. Many historians now consider him one of the first true scientists, because he insisted that every idea must be proved by careful experiments.

Decades later, Yusuf had become a respected teacher, and his students loved hearing about the madman who had never been mad at all. By then, the Book of Optics was being copied in libraries across the world, and centuries later, translated into Latin, it would inspire scientists in Europe who were searching for the same answers. Whenever a student asked him what the greatest lesson had been, Yusuf would close the shutters and let a single beam of light paint the street upside down on the wall. "He taught me that a mind locked in a dark room can still be free," he would say. "All you need is a small hole, a little courage and the patience to look."
